https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/tra.text: The Budapest Times Track record: government lays out rails-to-riches railway revival Written by Rainer Ackermann Around 3,500 billion forints (just over 9.6 billion euros) will be available over the next ten years for the "Gábor Baross" development plan to modernise the railway network. This was announced by Prime Minister Péter Magyar at the presentation of the Baross Plan on Wednesday in Budapest — in the presence of Transport Minister Dávid Vitézy — on the basis of a corresponding government decision from the previous week. He said the plan was far more than a purely transport project; it was about developing an entire national economy, connecting rural areas, improving workforce mobility, and advancing international division of labour. The Tisza leader wants modern rail to be understood as a programme behind which the nation can unite. Rail transport, as a time-saving, safe, and clean alternative to road travel, is gaining importance across Europe, and EU funding policy is aligned accordingly. In Hungary, the public’s desire to use rail as a mode of transport and mobility is growing steadily. The Prime Minister criticised the fact that János Lázár, the transport minister in the Orbán government, had treated the railways like a stepchild. The new government must now address backlogs that have accumulated over decades. The rolling stock of the state railway MÁV has an average age of 43 years, and a quarter of it is currently not operational. Nearly half of the rail carriages are not air-conditioned, and on 40% of the network, speed restrictions apply due to technical reasons. The Baross Plan pursues six core objectives that build on one another. The first concerns the optimal connection of all county towns with modern intercity trains, ideally on an hourly basis. In the longer term, an average speed of at least 100 km/h is to be achieved and guaranteed on main lines. The second concerns the development of a reliable regional network, including the modernisation of branch lines and coordinated timetables with Volán buses. Third, the agglomeration of Budapest and other major cities is to receive attractive rail services, including suburban rail and tram-train. Fourth, Budapest is to be highlighted as a strategic transport hub, as this is in the national interest. Fifth, rail freight must be modernised in order to reduce the burden on motorways caused by long-distance lorries. Sixth, the aim is better international connectivity, which includes rail links to the international airport “Ferenc Liszt” as well as the examination of international high-speed rail services (V4 project) and cross-border connections. Work will begin immediately on the comprehensive modernisation of the ten largest railway stations in the country and on the procurement of 35 intercity trains with a capacity of 400–500 passengers each and 42 suburban rail carriages each 120 metres in length, which are expected to arrive systematically from 2030 onwards. “This is not about isolated investments — it is about a genuinely modern, reliable and customer-oriented railway as a competitive alternative to the car,” the Prime Minister summarised. “We will actually invest the released EU funds in the interests of the people of this country,” said Transport Minister Dávid Vitézy. Since 1968 (!), the development of road transport had been the priority; the Tisza government is now putting an end to this approach. After only 20 billion forints flowed into modernisation under the railway-hostile Lázár, 1,100 billion forints from cohesion funds alone will flow by 2035, supplemented by 700 billion forints from the recovery fund, a European Investment Bank loan of 400 billion forints, the same amount from concessions, and 950 billion forints in EU funds expected to become available under the next financial framework for 2028–34. Specifically, metro line M3 is to be extended by two stations from Újpest-Centrum to Rákospalota-Újpest station by 2030. This would connect the M3 to the MÁV line — which runs northward toward the Danube Bend and onward into Slovakia — at a suburban point, in addition to its existing connection at the Western Railway Station in central Pest. The transport minister declined to rule out a later extension of the metro line to Káposztásmegyer at Budapest’s northern city boundary. Outside the capital, Debrecen’s main railway station is set to undergo comprehensive modernisation. The line from the eastern Hungarian metropolis to Balmazújváros will be electrified, while the line to Nyíregyháza will be upgraded to a speed of 160 km/h. The main line from Miskolc is to be connected to Budapest at a continuous speed of 160 km/h, and a tram-train project is being prepared between the industrial city and Kazincbarcika to the north as well as Tiszaújváros to the south. The standard speed between Budapest and Győr is also to reach 160 km/h. The main line between the capital and Szeged requires complete modernisation, while the dilapidated main line to Pécs leaves no option but new construction. https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/politics.text: Home Azerbaijan Politics Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry delivers protest note to Polish ambassador Politics News 28 August 2026 19:24 (UTC +04:00) Alamda Nasib Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 28. Poland's Ambassador to Azerbaijan Pawel Radomski was summoned to Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry, which delivered a protest note over a report broadcast by Polish public broadcaster TVP World. The Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry said the protest concerned a segment aired on the "Eastern Express" program on August 26, 2026, which it described as containing biased, inaccurate and "completely unacceptable" claims directed against the Azerbaijani state and its leadership, as well as provocative conduct by the program's host. The ministry said Azerbaijan expressed strong protest over the report and handed the Polish ambassador a formal note. "At a time when the normalization and peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia is underway, and Azerbaijan is making determined efforts to ensure lasting peace, stability and security in the region, the dissemination of information that distorts the truth raises questions on the Azerbaijani side," the ministry said. Azerbaijan described the broadcasting of negative content targeting the country by a public broadcaster funded by the Polish government as an "unfriendly step" that runs counter to the spirit of partnership between the two countries and could seriously harm bilateral relations. The Polish side was urged to take immediate and effective measures to stop such provocative campaigns targeting Azerbaijan," the ministry said. https://www.dw.com/en/france-macron-orde.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MrID The French president said Europe was facing more hybrid threats from Russia Image: Thomas Samson/AFP Advertisement French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday highlighted the threat of Russian hybrid attacks and called for measures to protect key infrastructure. "The Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," Macron said, adding that he had asked "the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure." The plan would also involve protecting the "most sensitive" defense industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks. What else did Macron say? Macron said that France would continue supporting Ukraine following Russia 's full-scale invasion in February 2022 and vowed to respond to Russia's shadow attacks. "This will not go unanswered," Macron said, without elaborating. "The intention behind it is to intimidate us and to derail the effort to support the Ukrainians. The consequence will be the opposite," he added. "We are not intimidated, because we know that what is at stake today in Ukraine is our security." How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video EU states concerned over Russian hybrid threat The comments come amid increasing concern from European states that Russia is ramping up hybrid threats that include acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and possible drone incursions. Poland, Germany and Denmark have in recent weeks accused Russia of being being a series of drone incursions as well as instances of sabotage, arson, and surveillance of defense facilities. Moscow has also been accused of planning to use a drone carrying explosives to attack an airport. Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU needed a mechanism similar to NATO that would allow for a better response to hybrid attacks blamed on Russia. The EU chief cited incidents such as an attempted drone attack on Leipzig last month that German authorities have attributed to Russia. Von der Leyen said the EU needed to develop "a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents ... that fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security."
